title: Prompting for Debugging
description: Learn the specific prompting techniques that turn AI into a debugging power tool — from stack traces to root cause analysis.

data.text: A great debugging prompt has four parts: the error message, the relevant code, what you expected, and what you have already tried. When all four are present, the AI can usually diagnose the problem in one or two turns. When one is missing, the AI will ask clarifying questions and waste time.

Paste the full error message, not just a summary. Include the stack trace — the AI uses the file names and line numbers in the trace to understand the call chain. A one-line error like 'undefined is not a function' is nearly useless without the stack trace that shows where it happened.

data.title: Paste the full stack trace
data.text: Developers often summarize the error when asking for help: 'I am getting a type error.' This is almost never enough for AI debugging. Paste the complete error message and full stack trace. The file names and line numbers in the trace are essential context.

Show the AI the code that is directly involved in the error — the function where the error occurs, plus the functions it calls. If the error is in a data transformation pipeline, show the entire pipeline, not just the function that throws. The AI needs to see the data flow to understand where it breaks.

Describe what you expected to happen in plain English, and what actually happened. 'I expected the list to be sorted alphabetically but it came back in insertion order' is much more useful than 'the sort is not working.' This gives the AI a hypothesis to test against the code.
Part 4: What You Have Already Tried

List the fixes you have already attempted and why they did not work. 'I tried adding a null check but the error moved to line 45' tells the AI something important: the null check was on the wrong variable, or there are multiple null values in the pipeline. This prevents the AI from suggesting the same fix again.

data.title: Templates for common debugging scenarios:
items: Type error: 'I am getting [error] at [file:line]. Here is the code: [code]. The expected type is [type] but the actual is [type]. What is causing this?'
Null/undefined: 'I am getting a TypeError because [variable] is undefined at [file:line]. Here is where it is set: [code]. What path leads to it being undefined?'
Performance: 'This function takes [time] instead of the expected [time]. Here is the code: [code]. I profiled it and the bottleneck is [operation]. How can I optimize this?'
Async/timing: 'I am getting a race condition where [description]. The async flow is: [sequence]. How should I restructure the promises/async-await?'

data.text: For hard bugs, use chain-of-thought prompting. Ask the AI to trace the execution path step by step before identifying the root cause. 'Walk through this code as if you were executing it with the input [input]. At each step, tell me what the variable values are. Stop when you find the discrepancy.'

data.title: An iterative debugging workflow:
items: Start with a structured debugging prompt (error + code + expected + tried)
If the error changes, paste the new error and what you changed
Once resolved, ask the AI to explain the root cause for your learning

data.title: Complete debugging prompt example
Use the AI to explain the fix
data.text: After the bug is fixed, ask the AI: 'Can you explain why fetchUser was not defined in this scope?' This turns a debugging session into a learning moment. Understanding the root cause prevents the same class of bug in the future.

data.title: Prompting for debugging
points: Always include the full error message and stack trace
Show the relevant code, not just the line that throws
List what you have already tried
Use chain-of-thought for hard bugs: ask for step-by-step reasoning
Learn from the fix: ask the AI to explain the root cause
